 The Role
 



  





 This is the first engineering hire, with one or two more expected to follow. You’ll own delivery of the entire product surface. The CEO is a working engineer who owns product and design and will be in the code alongside you — you’re not walking into a blank canvas, but it’s far from finished either.
 



  





 How the Team Builds
 



 Coding agents are the default way of working here, not an occasional assist — one engineer is covering what would conventionally take three, and that only works with real leverage. You won’t be asked to describe your workflow in the abstract; you’ll be handed a real problem and asked to solve it with whatever tools you normally use.
 



  





 As the first engineer, you’ll help set the conventions the next hires inherit — repo structure, agent context, test discipline, review norms. The standard: velocity is the point, but every line you ship should be something you can defend and explain.
 



  





 The team also values real technical debate. The CEO has been building solo up to this point, which means some architectural calls haven’t been pressure\-tested. This role is expected to push back, bring evidence, and help change minds when warranted — not simply implement decisions handed down.
 



  





  





 What You’ll Own
 



 • The member application — what a covered employee sees and uses: card, coverage, drug cost and where to get it.
 



 • The APIs and data model underneath the application.
 



 • Adjudication engine integration — eligibility ingestion from employers and TPAs, normalization, data pushes into the platform, daily claim extracts, and the reporting built on top. Data correctness matters a lot here; silent failures show up as real people getting turned away at a pharmacy counter.
 



 • Prior authorization plumbing — intake, criteria matching, routing, determination, and turnaround tracking. The CEO guides the clinical logic; you build the system it runs in.
 



 • Vendor integrations — drug data, specialty pharmacy partners, and others as the business grows.
 



 • The long tail — a genuinely long list of everything else, from interesting problems to the CSV that has to parse correctly at 6am.
 



  





  





 Sequencing
 



  





 Before the first live group in January, the bar is: eligibility in, claims out, a member can see their coverage, and a prior authorization can be received, routed, decided, and communicated. After that: the fuller member experience, price transparency, deeper vendor integrations, and self\-serve tooling.
 



  





 What This Role Is Not
 



 • Not a design role. The CEO owns product and design, and a design system already exists — you’ll build against it.
 



 • Not a blank canvas. Product direction is set; you’re not furnishing an empty room.
 



 • Not a research role. This is shipping, under deadline, in a regulated industry.
 



 You Probably
 



 • Have four to eight years building software.
 



 • Have a track record of shipping a surface area that seems disproportionate to your headcount and time — this is the strongest signal the team looks for.
 



 • Are backend\-leaning full stack, comfortable owning a data pipeline and a user\-facing app in the same week.
 



 • Have worked somewhere data correctness mattered and silent failure was expensive — regulated, financial, or infrastructure environments. Healthcare experience is a plus, not a requirement.
 



 • Are comfortable knowing nothing about pharmacy benefits going in, because you pick up new domains quickly.
 



 • Understand what it means — and what it costs — to be a company’s first engineer.
 



  





  





 Logistics
 



 In person in NYC
 



  





  





 Process
 



 1\. Intro call with the CEO — technical from the first minute.
 



  





 2\. Live pairing session (90 minutes) — a real repository, a real ticket, your own setup and tools. Nothing you write ships or is retained. This is about how you decompose a problem, what you verify versus trust, and how you catch subtle issues — no take\-home, no algorithm puzzles.
 



  





 3\. Domain reasoning exercise — you’ll work through a real claim rejection and plan design with no prior context. Nobody is expected to already know the answer; the team wants to see your approach.
 



  





 4\. References and offer.
